Chapter 7. The Power of Storytelling and the Burden of Bearing Witness.
You know, there’s a quiet kind of courage in telling the truth about what really happened. For so many who survived the war, sharing their stories wasn’t just a relief—it was a burden, too. Those memories were still raw, and saying them out loud made them real in a way that silence never could. But here’s the thing—there’s real power in bearing witness. By telling their stories, survivors could reclaim a piece of what the war tried to take from them.
Back in the rehabilitation center, storytelling was a tool for healing. But out in the world, it became something even bigger—a way to connect with others, to close the distance between those who’d lived through the war and those who hadn’t. Some survivors found themselves speaking at schools, at community events, even to journalists. Every time, remembering what happened was both painful and necessary.
Picture this: one afternoon, a young man stands in front of a group of students, his hands shaking as he begins. He describes the day his village was attacked, the fear as he ran, the moment someone handed him a gun. The room goes silent, everyone feeling the weight of his words. When he finishes, the questions start. Some are gentle, others hit straight to the heart. “How did you survive?” “Do you ever forgive yourself?” “What do you want people to know?”
He tries to answer, but the truth isn’t simple. Survival came at a cost. Forgiveness—it’s a work in progress. What he really wants is for people to understand: child soldiers aren’t monsters. They’re children who were forced into impossible situations. He wants people to see past the label, to recognize the humanity that war tried so hard to erase.
Telling his story leaves him exhausted, but it also brings a sense of relief. Each time he speaks, those memories lose a little of their hold on him. He realizes that silence was its own kind of prison—and sharing his experiences is a way to break free. Still, there’s a burden. Not everyone wants to listen. Some folks turn away, uncomfortable with the truth of what he’s been through. Others judge, unable—or unwilling—to see past the violence.
But he keeps telling his story. He sees the way it opens eyes, changes minds, sparks compassion. He meets other survivors, and together they build a community of witnesses. They support one another, sharing not just pain, but hope for the future. It becomes clear that storytelling isn’t just about the past—it’s about building a better future, one where survivors’ voices help make sure these horrors never happen again.
That’s the real power of storytelling. It connects people, builds understanding, and reminds the world that behind every statistic is a real human being with a story worth telling. For those who survived the war, bearing witness is both a responsibility and a gift—a way to honor what’s been lost, while helping to shape what’s still to come.
